title: Linked List Nodes

items.title: What is a Linked List Node?
items.content: A linked list is a linear data structure where elements are stored in nodes. Each node contains two main parts: data and a reference (pointer) to the next node in the sequence. The first node is called the head, and the last node points to None to mark the end. Understanding nodes is essential because every operation on a linked list—insertion, deletion, traversal—starts with manipulating these individual units. Think of a node as a box that holds a value and a link to the next box. Below is a simple Python implementation of a node class.
items.explanation: A linked list is a linear data structure where elements are stored in nodes. Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.prompt: Which of the following best describes the two components of a linked list node?
options: Data and a reference to the previous node
Data and a reference to the next node
items.correct_answer: Data and a reference to the next node
items.explanation: A linked list node stores data and a pointer (reference) to the next node. This structure allows the list to be traversed sequentially from the head to the tail.

items.prompt: What common mistake occurs when creating a node if you forget to set next to None in the __init__ method?
options: The node will store incorrect data
The node may retain a stale reference from a previous object, causing unexpected links
The program will raise a SyntaxError immediately
The node will automatically point to the head of the list
items.correct_answer: The node may retain a stale reference from a previous object, causing unexpected links
items.explanation: If next is not initialized to None, Python may leave an old reference in memory, which can accidentally connect nodes in unintended ways and corrupt the list structure.

items.prompt: The following code attempts to create a linked list node and append a new node, but it raises a runtime error. Identify the bug and explain why it occurs.
items.starter_code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

head = Node(10)
head.next = Node(20)
head.next.next = Node(30)

# Attempt to append
current = head
while current.next:
    current = current.next
current.next = Node(40)

print(head.data)
items.solution_code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

head = Node(10)
head.next = Node(20)
head.next.next = Node(30)

# Append safely
current = head
while current and current.next is not None:
    current = current.next
current.next = Node(40)

print(head.data)
items.hint: Check whether the loop condition correctly handles the end of the list and whether 'current' is ever set to 'None'.
items.explanation: The original loop condition 'while current.next' will raise an AttributeError when 'current' is 'None' if the list is empty or if 'current' becomes 'None' after the last node. The corrected version checks 'current' before accessing 'current.next', ensuring safe traversal to the tail of the linked list.

items.prompt: Fix the code so that it correctly initializes a linked list node with the given value and sets the 'next' pointer to 'None' by default.
items.hint: The default 'next' pointer for a new node should reference 'None', not an integer.
items.explanation: In a linked list node, 'next' must be 'None' to indicate the end of the list. Setting it to '0' is a logic error because '0' is a valid integer and would incorrectly link to a node with index 0. The fix changes 'self.next = 0' to 'self.next = None'.

items.prompt: The code below tries to insert a new node at the beginning of a linked list. It fails on an empty list. Correct the implementation to handle both empty and non-empty lists.
items.starter_code:
def insert_at_head(head, data):
    new_node = Node(data)
    new_node.next = head
    head = new_node
    return head

head = None
head = insert_at_head(head, 10)
print(head.data)
items.solution_code:
def insert_at_head(head, data):
    new_node = Node(data)
    new_node.next = head
    return new_node

head = None
head = insert_at_head(head, 10)
print(head.data)
items.hint: When inserting at the head, the function should return the new node as the new head, rather than trying to modify the caller's variable through assignment.
items.explanation: The original function correctly creates 'new_node' and links it, but the assignment 'head = new_node' only updates the local variable. In Python, reassigning a parameter does not affect the caller's reference. The fix returns 'new_node' directly, allowing the caller to update 'head'. This also works correctly when 'head' is 'None' because 'new_node.next = None' is valid.

items.prompt: A programmer wrote a function to print all values in a linked list. The code crashes with a 'NoneType' error. Locate the runtime error and describe the cause.
items.starter_code:
def print_list(head):
    current = head
    while current:
        print(current.data)
        current = current.next

head = Node(1)
head.next = Node(2)
head.next.next = None

print_list(head)
items.solution_code:
def print_list(head):
    current = head
    while current is not None:
        print(current.data)
        current = current.next

head = Node(1)
head.next = Node(2)
head.next.next = None

print_list(head)
items.hint: Consider what happens when 'current' becomes 'None' and the loop condition is evaluated.
items.explanation: The loop condition 'while current' evaluates to 'False' when 'current' is 'None', so the loop terminates before attempting to access 'current.data'. However, if the condition were written as 'while current.next' or if 'current' were reassigned after the last node, accessing 'current.data' on 'None' would raise a 'NoneType' error. The corrected condition 'while current is not None' explicitly checks for termination and is clearer. In this specific starter code, the bug is subtle: the loop actually works, but if 'current' were ever 'None' before the check, 'current.data' would fail. The fix ensures the guard is explicit.

items.prompt: The following deletion function is supposed to remove the first occurrence of a value from a linked list. It has a logic error that causes it to skip nodes or lose references. Repair the code.
items.starter_code:
def delete_node(head, key):
    current = head
    prev = None
    while current and current.data != key:
        prev = current
        current = current.next
    if current is None:
        return head
    prev.next = current.next
    return head

head = Node(10)
head.next = Node(20)
head.next.next = Node(30)
head = delete_node(head, 20)
print(head.next.data)
items.solution_code:
def delete_node(head, key):
    current = head
    prev = None
    while current and current.data != key:
        prev = current
        current = current.next
    if current is None:
        return head
    if prev is None:
        return current.next
    prev.next = current.next
    return head

head = Node(10)
head.next = Node(20)
head.next.next = Node(30)
head = delete_node(head, 20)
print(head.next.data)
items.hint: When the node to delete is the head, 'prev' remains 'None'. The current code attempts to set 'None.next', which raises an AttributeError.
items.explanation: The original code fails when 'key' matches the 'head' node because 'prev' is still 'None'. Setting 'prev.next = current.next' would raise 'AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'next'. The repair adds a check: if 'prev is None', return 'current.next' directly, making the new head the next node. This preserves list integrity for head deletion, middle deletion, and tail deletion.

items.prompt: Refactor the linked list implementation below to use a sentinel (dummy) head node. This should simplify insertion, deletion, and traversal by eliminating special-case handling for the head. Provide the refactored class and core methods.

test_cases.input: ll = LinkedList(); ll.append(10); ll.append(20); ll.append(30); ll.delete(20); print(ll.display())
ll = LinkedList(); ll.append(1); ll.append(2); ll.append(3); ll.delete(1); print(ll.display())

items.hint: Create a dummy node in __init__ that never stores user data. All real nodes follow it, so head insertions and deletions no longer need to check for 'None'.
items.explanation: The sentinel head eliminates the need for separate 'if self.head is None' checks. In append, traversal always starts at the sentinel and stops at the last real node. In delete, we only look at 'current.next', so removing the head is identical to removing any other node: we simply skip 'current.next'. The display method starts at 'self.head.next' to skip the sentinel. This reduces branching logic, lowers the chance of off-by-one or null-reference bugs, and makes the code more maintainable.
